Front: [MHC] Which cells express MHC I, and which T cells recognize it?
Back:
Answer: Nearly all nucleated cells express MHC I; CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize peptide-MHC I complexes.

Why it matters: Because MHC I is present on nearly every nucleated cell, it lets CD8 cells inspect cells for intracellular infection or malignant change. Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus and do not express MHC I.

PDF page(s): 3-5, 9-10

Front: [MHC] Which cells express MHC II, and which T cells recognize it?
Back:
Answer: Professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) express MHC II; CD4+ helper T cells recognize peptide-MHC II complexes.

Why it matters: These professional APCs take up extracellular material and present it to helper T cells. CD4 binds MHC II and helps stabilize the interaction while the TCR recognizes the specific peptide.

PDF page(s): 3, 5, 10

Front: [MHC] What antigen source is usually presented on MHC I versus MHC II?
Back:
Answer: MHC I presents endogenous/intracellular peptides (e.g., viral proteins); MHC II presents exogenous peptides taken up into endosomes.

Why it matters: Endogenous proteins enter the cytosolic processing pathway; exogenous proteins are engulfed and processed in vesicles. This distinction predicts which T-cell arm responds: CD8 for MHC I, CD4 for MHC II.

PDF page(s): 3, 27-28

Front: [MHC] What is the key processing route for MHC I peptides?
Back:
Answer: Cytosolic proteins are degraded by the proteasome; peptides enter the ER via TAP and load onto MHC I associated with beta-2-microglobulin.

Why it matters: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum. There they associate with MHC I and beta-2-microglobulin before the complex moves to the surface.

PDF page(s): 3, 27-28

Front: [MHC] How are peptides loaded onto MHC II?
Back:
Answer: MHC II travels with invariant chain; after its cleavage in an acidified endosome, exogenous peptides load onto MHC II.

Why it matters: Invariant chain prevents premature peptide binding in the ER and directs MHC II toward endosomal compartments. Acidic processing removes the chain so peptides from engulfed antigens can load.

PDF page(s): 3, 27-28

Front: [Tcells] What are the two signals for naive T-cell activation?
Back:
Answer: Signal 1: TCR plus CD4 or CD8 binds peptide-MHC. Signal 2: B7 (CD80/CD86) on the APC binds CD28 on the T cell.

Why it matters: Signal 1 provides antigen specificity; signal 2 confirms that an APC is activating the naive T cell. Without costimulation, antigen recognition alone may cause anergy rather than full activation.

PDF page(s): 5, 17-18

Front: [Tcells] What is the main effector function of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells?
Back:
Answer: They kill infected or malignant cells displaying antigen on MHC I, using perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis.

Why it matters: Perforin helps deliver granzymes into the target cell, activating apoptosis. This is a cell-mediated mechanism and does not require antibody.

PDF page(s): 4-5, 10

Front: [Tcells] What is the key function of Th1 cells?
Back:
Answer: Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma to activate macrophages and support cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens.

Why it matters: IFN-gamma activates macrophages to kill ingested microbes and can promote granuloma formation. Th1 responses are especially useful when pathogens survive inside host cells.

PDF page(s): 6-8, 10

Front: [Tcells] What is the key function of Th2 cells?
Back:
Answer: Th2 cells help activate B cells and promote antibody production; CD40L-CD40 interaction supports B-cell activation and class switching.

Why it matters: Th2 cells provide help to B cells through cytokines and CD40L binding CD40. This promotes plasma-cell differentiation, antibody production, and class switching.

PDF page(s): 6-8, 10

Front: [Tcells] What does Th17 chiefly promote?
Back:
Answer: Neutrophil production and recruitment.

Why it matters: IL-17 from Th17 cells promotes inflammatory signals that recruit neutrophils. This makes Th17 important for defense against many extracellular bacteria and fungi.

PDF page(s): 6, 17

Front: [Tcells] What is the role of regulatory T cells?
Back:
Answer: They suppress immune responses and help maintain self-tolerance; CD25 is a common Treg marker.

Why it matters: Tregs restrain excessive immune activation and help prevent responses against self. Loss of regulatory function can contribute to autoimmunity.

PDF page(s): 6, 17

Front: [Tcells] What cytokine loop links Th1 cells and macrophages?
Back:
Answer: Macrophage IL-12 promotes Th1 differentiation and IFN-gamma secretion; IFN-gamma activates macrophages, which produce more IL-12.

Why it matters: This reciprocal signaling amplifies cell-mediated defense: IL-12 pushes Th0 cells toward Th1, and Th1-derived IFN-gamma activates macrophages to make more IL-12.

PDF page(s): 7-8, 17

Front: [Tcells] What cytokines favor Th2 differentiation?
Back:
Answer: IL-4 and IL-10 favor Th2 differentiation; Th2 supports B-cell activation and humoral immunity.

Why it matters: IL-4 and IL-10 bias helper differentiation toward Th2 and away from Th1. Th2 support is associated with B-cell antibody responses, including IgE-related allergic and parasite responses.

PDF page(s): 7-8, 16-17

Front: [Tcells] What are positive and negative selection in the thymus?
Back:
Answer: Positive selection in the cortex preserves T cells able to recognize self-MHC. Negative selection in the medulla removes strongly self-reactive T cells.

Why it matters: Positive selection tests whether the developing T cell can recognize self-MHC; negative selection removes cells that react too strongly to self-antigens. The sequence establishes MHC restriction while reducing autoimmunity.

PDF page(s): 9-10

Front: [Innate] How do NK cells detect some virus-infected or tumor cells?
Back:
Answer: They can kill cells with reduced MHC I expression, a missing-self signal.

Why it matters: Many infected or tumor cells reduce MHC I to evade CD8 recognition. NK cells detect this loss of inhibitory self-signaling and can kill the abnormal cell.

PDF page(s): 3-4

Front: [Innate] How does CD16 enable NK-cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity?
Back:
Answer: CD16 binds the Fc portion of IgG coating a target; NK-cell activation releases cytotoxic granules and induces apoptosis.

Why it matters: CD16 is an Fc receptor. When it binds IgG already attached to a target, the NK cell is activated and kills the antibody-coated cell; this is ADCC.

PDF page(s): 4, 17

Front: [Antibodies] Which antibody is usually produced first in a primary immune response?
Back:
Answer: IgM; its presence can indicate recent infection, depending on context.

Why it matters: IgM is the first major antibody in a primary response and is usually too large to cross the placenta. A newborn's IgM is therefore evidence of the infant's own response rather than maternal IgG transfer.

PDF page(s): 12-13

Front: [Antibodies] Which antibody is a pentamer and has the greatest avidity?
Back:
Answer: IgM is generally secreted as a pentamer and has high avidity because it can bind multiple epitopes.

Why it matters: Pentameric IgM has many antigen-binding sites, giving high avidity even if each individual binding interaction is not the tightest. It also efficiently activates the classical complement pathway.

PDF page(s): 12

Front: [Antibodies] Which antibody is most abundant in serum and crosses the placenta?
Back:
Answer: IgG. It mediates passive neonatal immunity and can cause Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn.

Why it matters: IgG is the predominant serum antibody and the only immunoglobulin class that normally crosses the placenta in meaningful amounts. Maternal anti-Rh IgG can cross and hemolyze fetal RBCs.

PDF page(s): 12, 22, 36

Front: [Antibodies] Which antibody predominates in mucosal secretions and breast milk?
Back:
Answer: IgA, typically secreted as a dimer linked by a J chain.

Why it matters: Secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces in respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and is transported into breast milk. It helps neutralize pathogens at entry sites.

PDF page(s): 12-13

Front: [Antibodies] Which antibody is associated with mast cells, immediate allergy, and helminths?
Back:
Answer: IgE binds Fc receptors on mast cells; allergen cross-linking triggers degranulation. IgE also supports eosinophil responses to helminths.

Why it matters: Allergen cross-linking of IgE bound to mast-cell Fc receptors triggers histamine and other mediator release. IgE also helps recruit eosinophil-mediated responses against helminths.

PDF page(s): 13, 24

Front: [Antibodies] How does active immunity differ from passive immunity?
Back:
Answer: Active immunity follows antigen exposure and creates memory, so develops more slowly but lasts longer. Passive immunity transfers preformed antibodies, acts quickly, and wanes.

Why it matters: Vaccination or infection creates the host's own response and memory. Transferred antibody gives immediate protection but fades as the antibody is cleared and does not create memory in the recipient.

PDF page(s): 13

Front: [Antibodies] What is affinity maturation?
Back:
Answer: Germinal-center B cells undergo somatic hypermutation and selection, producing antibodies with increased affinity for antigen.

Why it matters: Somatic hypermutation introduces immunoglobulin gene mutations in activated germinal-center B cells. Selection favors B cells whose antibodies bind antigen better, increasing affinity over time.

PDF page(s): 4, 8

Front: [Antibodies] How does V(D)J recombination differ from somatic hypermutation?
Back:
Answer: V(D)J recombination creates receptor diversity during lymphocyte development; somatic hypermutation later diversifies immunoglobulin genes in activated B cells.

Why it matters: V(D)J recombination occurs during B- and T-cell development to assemble receptor genes. Somatic hypermutation occurs later in activated B cells and affects antibody variable regions, not TCRs.

PDF page(s): 8

Front: [Antibodies] What is the main defect in CD40L deficiency (hyper-IgM syndrome)?
Back:
Answer: Impaired T-cell help to B cells causes defective class switching; IgM is normal or elevated while other isotypes are low.

Why it matters: CD40L on an activated helper T cell binds CD40 on a B cell, normally enabling class-switch recombination. Without this help, B cells remain largely IgM-producing and are impaired in responses to many pathogens.

PDF page(s): 12, 18, 27

Front: [Complement] Which complement pathways are activated by antibody, microbial surfaces, and mannose-binding lectin?
Back:
Answer: Classical: antibody-bound antigen (IgM or IgG); alternative: microbial surfaces; lectin: mannose-binding lectin binding microbial carbohydrates.

Why it matters: The classical pathway begins when C1 binds antibody-coated antigen; alternative activation occurs on microbial surfaces; lectin activation begins with mannose-binding lectin. All converge on complement activation.

PDF page(s): 14

Front: [Complement] What is the membrane attack complex, and which components form it?
Back:
Answer: MAC is the C5b-C9 complex that forms membrane pores and can lyse target cells.

Why it matters: C5b initiates assembly of C6, C7, C8, and C9 into a pore. MAC is particularly important for lysis of susceptible gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria.

PDF page(s): 14-15

Front: [Complement] What are the two major opsonins?
Back:
Answer: C3b and IgG; they coat targets and promote phagocytosis.

Why it matters: Opsonins coat microbes so phagocytes can recognize and ingest them efficiently. IgG binds Fc receptors, while C3b is recognized by complement receptors.

PDF page(s): 14

Front: [Complement] Which complement fragments are anaphylatoxins?
Back:
Answer: C3a, C4a, and C5a. C5a is also a potent neutrophil chemoattractant.

Why it matters: C3a, C4a, and C5a promote inflammation and mast-cell degranulation. C5a also recruits neutrophils, so it has an important chemotactic role beyond anaphylatoxin activity.

PDF page(s): 14

Front: [Complement] What infection pattern suggests terminal complement (C5-C9) deficiency?
Back:
Answer: Recurrent Neisseria infections, including meningococcal disease and disseminated gonococcal infection, due to impaired MAC formation.

Why it matters: Loss of C5-C9 prevents effective MAC formation. Recurrent Neisseria is the characteristic clue; total hemolytic complement activity can be low.

PDF page(s): 14, 27, 30

Front: [Complement] What is the complement defect in hereditary angioedema?
Back:
Answer: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes excess bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

Why it matters: C1 inhibitor normally restrains contact-system and complement pathways. Deficiency increases bradykinin, causing episodic swelling without urticaria; airway involvement can be dangerous.

PDF page(s): 15

Front: [Complement] Which RBC-protective proteins are lost in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
Back:
Answer: CD55 and CD59, which are GPI-anchored complement regulators; their loss permits complement-mediated RBC lysis.

Why it matters: CD55 accelerates decay of complement convertases and CD59 blocks MAC formation. Their GPI-anchor deficiency allows complement to lyse RBCs, producing intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria.

PDF page(s): 15, 18

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine is most associated with hypotension in septic shock?
Back:
Answer: TNF-alpha, which increases vascular permeability and lowers systemic vascular resistance.

Why it matters: TNF-alpha is a major mediator of distributive shock through vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. If asked for the cytokine causing fever specifically, IL-1 is the stronger association.

PDF page(s): 16, 33, 38

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine is classically associated with fever during infection?
Back:
Answer: IL-1. Antipyretic NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin synthesis downstream in the fever pathway.

Why it matters: IL-1 acts through pathways that raise hypothalamic prostaglandin E2 and the temperature set point. NSAIDs lower fever by reducing prostaglandin synthesis rather than directly blocking IL-1.

PDF page(s): 16, 38-39

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine broadly stimulates T-cell proliferation?
Back:
Answer: IL-2.

Why it matters: IL-2 is produced by activated T cells and promotes T-cell growth and proliferation. Calcineurin inhibitors reduce IL-2 transcription, while sirolimus blocks downstream response to IL-2.

PDF page(s): 16-17

Front: [Drugs] How do cyclosporine and tacrolimus reduce T-cell activation?
Back:
Answer: They inhibit calcineurin, reducing IL-2 transcription. Cyclosporine binds cyclophilin; tacrolimus binds FKBP.

Why it matters: Calcineurin normally promotes NFAT-mediated IL-2 transcription. Cyclosporine-cyclophilin and tacrolimus-FKBP complexes inhibit calcineurin; both suppress T-cell activation and can be nephrotoxic.

PDF page(s): 16, 42-43

Front: [Drugs] How does sirolimus affect IL-2 signaling?
Back:
Answer: It inhibits mTOR and reduces T-cell responsiveness to IL-2 rather than blocking IL-2 transcription.

Why it matters: Sirolimus forms a complex with FKBP that inhibits mTOR. Unlike tacrolimus, it does not inhibit calcineurin; it blocks the T cell's response to IL-2.

PDF page(s): 16, 43

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine is a major neutrophil chemoattractant?
Back:
Answer: IL-8 (CXCL8). Other chemoattractants include C5a, LTB4, and bacterial products.

Why it matters: IL-8 is a chemokine that draws neutrophils toward inflamed tissue. C5a, leukotriene B4, and bacterial products also guide neutrophil migration.

PDF page(s): 16-17, 40

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine promotes eosinophil maturation?
Back:
Answer: IL-5.

Why it matters: IL-5 supports eosinophil differentiation and activation. This is relevant to allergic disease and helminth defense, where eosinophils release toxic granule proteins.

PDF page(s): 16

Front: [Cytokines] Which cytokine promotes hepatic acute-phase protein production?
Back:
Answer: IL-6, which supports production of proteins such as CRP and hepcidin.

Why it matters: IL-6 stimulates hepatocytes to produce acute-phase reactants such as CRP and hepcidin. It also participates in inflammatory T-cell differentiation pathways.

PDF page(s): 16

Front: [Cytokines] What is the key effect of IFN-gamma?
Back:
Answer: It activates macrophages and supports Th1 responses; it is important for granuloma formation and control of intracellular pathogens.

Why it matters: IFN-gamma is the key macrophage-activating cytokine in Th1 immunity. If IL-12/IFN-gamma signaling is disrupted, control of intracellular pathogens and granuloma formation can be impaired.

PDF page(s): 7, 17, 40-41

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What is the classic infection pattern in SCID?
Back:
Answer: Early severe infections spanning viral, fungal, bacterial, and protozoal pathogens, with combined T- and B-cell dysfunction.

Why it matters: Combined T- and B-cell dysfunction explains the broad pathogen range and severe early disease. A small thymus suggests T-cell deficiency; sparse tonsils or lymph nodes suggest poor B-cell development.

PDF page(s): 25, 28, 32-34

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What are common genetic causes of SCID?
Back:
Answer: X-linked common gamma-chain/IL-2 receptor pathway defects and autosomal recessive ADA deficiency are classic causes.

Why it matters: Common gamma-chain defects impair signaling through several cytokine receptors, including the IL-2 receptor pathway; ADA deficiency is another classic cause. Severe combined defects require specialist management and often stem-cell transplantation.

PDF page(s): 25

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease)?
Back:
Answer: BTK mutation blocks B-cell maturation. Recurrent bacterial infections often begin after maternal IgG wanes, around 6 months.

Why it matters: BTK is required for B-cell maturation, so circulating B cells and all immunoglobulin classes are low. The timing after maternal IgG wanes explains why infections often emerge after early infancy.

PDF page(s): 25, 28, 32-33

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What infection pattern is associated with selective IgA deficiency?
Back:
Answer: Recurrent sinopulmonary and mucosal infections; Giardia and atopy are also associated. Other immunoglobulin classes may be preserved.

Why it matters: IgA protects mucosal surfaces, so deficiency can cause respiratory infections and GI susceptibility such as Giardia. Atopy and autoimmune disease are also associated; isolated IgA deficiency leaves other classes relatively intact.

PDF page(s): 12-13, 25, 28

Front: [Immunodeficiency] Why can IgA deficiency cause a false-negative celiac serology?
Back:
Answer: IgA-based tests such as tissue-transglutaminase IgA may be falsely negative; use an IgG-based test when IgA deficiency is present.

Why it matters: If total IgA is absent, an IgA-based screening assay may not detect disease even when it is present. An IgG-based celiac assay is useful in that setting.

PDF page(s): 12-13, 25

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What causes DiGeorge syndrome and its classic immunologic defect?
Back:
Answer: 22q11 deletion with abnormal development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches causes thymic hypoplasia and T-cell deficiency.

Why it matters: Thymic hypoplasia reduces T-cell maturation. The embryologic pouch defect also affects parathyroid development, linking immune findings with hypocalcemia.

PDF page(s): 25, 33-34

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What findings are associated with DiGeorge syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia, conotruncal cardiac defects, and an absent or small thymic shadow.

Why it matters: Parathyroid hypoplasia can cause hypocalcemia and tetany; conotruncal defects such as tetralogy of Fallot can co-occur. These clues plus absent thymic shadow point to DiGeorge syndrome.

PDF page(s): 25, 33-34

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What causes chronic granulomatous disease, and which organisms are characteristic?
Back:
Answer: NADPH oxidase deficiency impairs respiratory-burst superoxide production, predisposing to catalase-positive organisms such as Staph aureus, Serratia, Aspergillus, and Candida.

Why it matters: NADPH oxidase normally generates superoxide during the respiratory burst. Catalase-positive microbes destroy their own hydrogen peroxide, so they can survive when the patient's oxidative burst is defective.

PDF page(s): 26, 35-36

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What test is used to diagnose chronic granulomatous disease?
Back:
Answer: Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry shows reduced oxidative burst.

Why it matters: Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry measures neutrophil oxidative burst; fluorescence is reduced in CGD. It is the preferred modern test over the older nitroblue tetrazolium assay.

PDF page(s): 26, 36

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What is deficient in myeloperoxidase deficiency?
Back:
Answer: Conversion of hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid/bleach is impaired; Candida infections are a classic association.

Why it matters: Myeloperoxidase uses hydrogen peroxide and chloride to form hypochlorous acid, a potent antimicrobial oxidant. Many patients are asymptomatic, but Candida infection is a classic association.

PDF page(s): 26, 36

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What is the classic triad of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Immunodeficiency, eczema, and thrombocytopenia; it is X-linked and involves defective WASp-mediated cytoskeletal signaling.

Why it matters: WASp helps organize actin in hematopoietic cells. Defective signaling impairs immune-cell function and platelet production/size, producing the characteristic eczema-infection-thrombocytopenia triad.

PDF page(s): 26-27, 37

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1?
Back:
Answer: CD18 (beta-2 integrin) deficiency impairs firm adhesion and extravasation, causing recurrent infections, little/no pus, neutrophilia, and sometimes delayed umbilical-cord separation.

Why it matters: LFA-1 integrin uses CD18 for firm leukocyte adhesion to endothelium. Failure to exit vessels causes neutrophilia in blood but few neutrophils and little pus at infected tissues.

PDF page(s): 26, 28-29, 32

Front: [Innate] Which molecules mediate leukocyte rolling, firm adhesion, and diapedesis?
Back:
Answer: Rolling: selectins. Firm adhesion: integrins (e.g., LFA-1). Diapedesis: PECAM-1 (CD31).

Why it matters: Selectins mediate rolling, integrins mediate firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 supports passage between endothelial cells. This sequence explains the stages of leukocyte extravasation.

PDF page(s): 29

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome?
Back:
Answer: LYST-related lysosomal trafficking dysfunction impairs phagolysosome fusion; findings include recurrent infections, giant granules, partial albinism, and sometimes neuropathy.

Why it matters: Defective lysosomal trafficking disrupts phagolysosome fusion and microbial killing. Abnormal melanosome transport causes partial albinism; giant granules in leukocytes are a key smear clue.

PDF page(s): 26, 32, 34

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What are hallmark findings of hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Elevated IgE, eczema, recurrent cold Staph abscesses, coarse facies, and retained primary teeth (FATED mnemonic).

Why it matters: Job syndrome classically involves impaired Th17-related defense and recurrent staphylococcal skin/lung infections. 'Cold' abscesses, eczema, retained primary teeth, and elevated IgE are useful clues.

PDF page(s): 13, 27, 37

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What immunodeficiency is associated with recurrent mucocutaneous Candida and autoimmune disease?
Back:
Answer: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis due to T-cell dysfunction and impaired cell-mediated immunity.

Why it matters: Impaired T-cell-mediated defense permits recurrent Candida of skin and mucosa. Autoimmune endocrinopathies can coexist, so candidiasis plus type 1 diabetes or thyroiditis is a high-yield pattern.

PDF page(s): 26, 28, 34, 37

Front: [Immunodeficiency] What pathway explains recurrent TB with IL-12 receptor deficiency?
Back:
Answer: Reduced IL-12 signaling lowers Th1 IFN-gamma production and macrophage activation.

Why it matters: IL-12 normally stimulates Th1 cells to produce IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages. Defects anywhere in this loop impair granuloma-based control of mycobacteria.

PDF page(s): 17, 27, 40-41

Front: [Immunodeficiency] How does CVID differ from selective IgA deficiency?
Back:
Answer: CVID involves impaired B-cell differentiation into plasma cells and low levels of multiple immunoglobulin classes; selective IgA deficiency chiefly lowers IgA.

Why it matters: CVID generally causes low IgG plus low levels of other antibody classes due to poor antibody production despite B cells being present. Selective IgA deficiency is limited primarily to IgA.

PDF page(s): 27

Front: [Hypersensitivity] What is the mechanism of type I hypersensitivity?
Back:
Answer: Immediate IgE-mediated mast-cell/basophil degranulation within minutes; a later eosinophil-rich phase can develop over hours.

Why it matters: IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation explains rapid urticaria, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis. The late phase reflects recruited inflammatory cells, especially eosinophils.

PDF page(s): 13, 24

Front: [Hypersensitivity] What is the mechanism of type II hypersensitivity?
Back:
Answer: IgG or IgM binds cell-surface or matrix antigens, or alters receptor function; injury can involve complement, opsonization, or altered signaling.

Why it matters: Type II antibodies bind fixed targets on cells or tissues. They may destroy cells, alter receptor activity, or trigger inflammation; examples include Graves, Goodpasture, and autoimmune hemolysis.

PDF page(s): 24

Front: [Hypersensitivity] What is the mechanism of type III hypersensitivity?
Back:
Answer: Circulating antigen-antibody immune complexes deposit in tissues and activate inflammation/complement.

Why it matters: In type III disease, soluble immune complexes deposit in vessel walls, glomeruli, or joints and activate complement. This differs from type II, where antibody binds a fixed tissue target.

PDF page(s): 24, 42

Front: [Hypersensitivity] What is the mechanism of type IV hypersensitivity?
Back:
Answer: T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity; it does not require antibodies. Examples include contact dermatitis, PPD reaction, and graft-versus-host disease.

Why it matters: Type IV reactions are driven by sensitized T cells and take time to develop. PPD induration and poison ivy dermatitis are classic examples; antibodies are not the primary mechanism.

PDF page(s): 24, 39, 42

Front: [Hypersensitivity] Which hypersensitivity mechanism causes post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
Back:
Answer: Type III immune-complex deposition.

Why it matters: PSGN follows streptococcal infection because deposited immune complexes activate complement in glomeruli. This is distinct from rheumatic fever, where antibodies cross-react with host tissue (type II).

PDF page(s): 14, 22, 24

Front: [Autoimmunity] What distinguishes bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus vulgaris?
Back:
Answer: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes at the basement membrane (subepidermal blister, linear IF); pemphigus vulgaris targets desmogleins in desmosomes (intraepidermal blister, net-like IF, often positive Nikolsky sign).

Why it matters: BP antibodies target hemidesmosomes, splitting below the epidermis; PV antibodies target desmosomes between keratinocytes, causing intraepidermal separation. The biopsy staining pattern reflects the target's location.

PDF page(s): 18

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibodies and biopsy pattern are associated with Goodpasture syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen; renal biopsy shows linear immunofluorescence.

Why it matters: Type IV collagen is present in basement membranes, so anti-GBM antibodies affect both glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Linear staining follows the continuous distribution of the antigen.

PDF page(s): 18-19

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibodies are associated with GPA versus EGPA?
Back:
Answer: GPA: c-ANCA/anti-PR3. EGPA: p-ANCA/anti-MPO, often with asthma and eosinophilia.

Why it matters: GPA commonly causes granulomatous inflammation of upper/lower airways and kidneys with PR3/c-ANCA. EGPA combines asthma and eosinophilia with MPO/p-ANCA association.

PDF page(s): 19

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibody is highly specific for SLE, and which tracks lupus nephritis activity?
Back:
Answer: Anti-Smith is highly specific; anti-dsDNA correlates with flares and renal disease activity. C3 can fall during active disease.

Why it matters: Anti-dsDNA levels often rise with active lupus nephritis and can track disease activity. Anti-Smith is less sensitive but highly specific; complement can be consumed during active immune-complex disease.

PDF page(s): 19

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibodies are associated with antiphospholipid syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Anticardiolipin, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I, and lupus anticoagulant; they are associated with thrombosis and recurrent pregnancy loss. Lupus anticoagulant prolongs in-vitro aPTT.

Why it matters: These antibodies are associated with arterial/venous thrombosis and pregnancy morbidity despite a prolonged in-vitro clotting test. The lupus anticoagulant name is misleading: clinically it promotes clotting.

PDF page(s): 18-19

Front: [Autoimmunity] What antibodies are associated with myasthenia gravis versus Lambert-Eaton syndrome?
Back:
Answer: Myasthenia gravis: postsynaptic nicotinic ACh-receptor antibodies. Lambert-Eaton: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies.

Why it matters: MG antibodies impair postsynaptic neuromuscular transmission and weakness worsens with use. Lambert-Eaton antibodies reduce presynaptic ACh release, and strength may improve with repeated activity.

PDF page(s): 20

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibodies are associated with limited versus diffuse systemic sclerosis?
Back:
Answer: Limited/CREST: anti-centromere. Diffuse disease: anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70).

Why it matters: Limited systemic sclerosis is linked to anti-centromere and CREST features. Diffuse disease is linked to anti-Scl-70 and more extensive skin/organ involvement, including pulmonary fibrosis.

PDF page(s): 20

Front: [Autoimmunity] Which antibodies are associated with Graves disease versus Hashimoto thyroiditis?
Back:
Answer: Graves: TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies (TSI). Hashimoto: anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin.

Why it matters: TSI stimulates the TSH receptor and causes hyperthyroidism. Hashimoto antibodies accompany autoimmune thyroid destruction and hypothyroidism.

PDF page(s): 20-21

Front: [Autoimmunity] What causes warm versus cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
Back:
Answer: Warm AIHA: IgG. Cold agglutinin AIHA: IgM, often associated with Mycoplasma or viral infections such as EBV/CMV.

Why it matters: Warm IgG binds RBCs at body temperature; cold IgM binds at cooler temperatures and may agglutinate RBCs. Both can cause a positive direct antiglobulin test.

PDF page(s): 22, 39

Front: [Antibodies] How does Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn occur?
Back:
Answer: An Rh-negative mother sensitized to Rh-positive fetal RBCs can produce anti-D IgG; in a later pregnancy, IgG crosses the placenta and destroys fetal RBCs.

Why it matters: Initial maternal exposure sensitizes an Rh-negative mother; anti-D IgG in a later pregnancy crosses the placenta. Rho(D) immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization when appropriately administered.

PDF page(s): 12, 22, 36

Front: [Transfusion] What causes an acute ABO-incompatible transfusion reaction?
Back:
Answer: Recipient antibodies bind donor RBC A/B antigens, activating complement and causing intravascular hemolysis; direct antiglobulin (Coombs) testing is typically positive.

Why it matters: Preformed recipient anti-A or anti-B antibodies activate complement against donor RBCs, causing rapid intravascular hemolysis. Stop the transfusion immediately and evaluate with a direct antiglobulin test.

PDF page(s): 23

Front: [Transfusion] What causes a febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction?
Back:
Answer: Recipient antibodies react with donor leukocytes or leukocyte-derived cytokines, causing fever/chills without RBC hemolysis; leukoreduction lowers risk.

Why it matters: Leukocyte antibodies or cytokines cause fever and chills, but donor RBCs are not being destroyed. This contrasts with acute ABO hemolysis; leukoreduced products reduce the reaction risk.

PDF page(s): 22-23

Front: [Transfusion] How can you distinguish TRALI from TACO after transfusion?
Back:
Answer: Both cause acute pulmonary edema. TRALI is noncardiogenic and usually begins within 6 hours; TACO is volume-overload/cardiogenic and is more likely with heart failure or later onset.

Why it matters: TRALI results from neutrophil-mediated lung injury and is noncardiogenic; TACO reflects excess hydrostatic pressure from volume overload. Timing and heart-failure history help separate them.

Front: [Hypersensitivity] What is the Arthus reaction?
Back:
Answer: A localized type III immune-complex reaction at an exposure site, typically developing hours to days after exposure.

Why it matters: Arthus reaction is a local immune-complex response after antigen exposure in a sensitized person. Local vasculitis and tissue inflammation develop over hours, rather than the immediate timing of type I allergy.

Front: [Vaccines] Why are polysaccharide vaccines often conjugated to protein?
Back:
Answer: Pure polysaccharides elicit a largely T-cell-independent B-cell response with limited memory; protein conjugation enables MHC II presentation and T-cell help, improving class switching and memory.

Why it matters: Polysaccharides alone are T-independent antigens and generate weaker memory, especially in young children. A protein carrier can be presented on MHC II to recruit helper T cells and improve durable antibody responses.

Front: [Vaccines] What is the difference between a toxoid vaccine and a conjugate vaccine?
Back:
Answer: A toxoid uses an inactivated protein toxin (e.g., tetanus or diphtheria). A conjugate vaccine links a polysaccharide antigen to a protein carrier to recruit T-cell help (e.g., Hib, pneumococcal, meningococcal).

Why it matters: Toxoids are inactivated protein toxins that induce neutralizing antibodies against toxin effects. Conjugate vaccines attach a bacterial polysaccharide to a protein carrier to enable T-cell help.

PDF page(s): 15

Front: [Vaccines] What immune responses are generally produced by live-attenuated versus inactivated vaccines?
Back:
Answer: Live-attenuated vaccines can replicate intracellularly and stimulate cellular and humoral immunity. Inactivated vaccines mainly stimulate humoral responses and often require boosters/adjuvants.

Why it matters: Live organisms can enter host cells and generate MHC I presentation as well as antibody responses. Inactivated vaccines cannot replicate and mainly induce antibody responses, often needing boosters.

Front: [Transplant] What is the defining mechanism of graft-versus-host disease?
Back:
Answer: Donor T cells recognize recipient tissues as foreign and attack them; classically follows hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and is cell-mediated (type IV).

Why it matters: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor immunocompetent T cells attack recipient tissues they recognize as foreign. Skin, gut, and liver are common targets after marrow transplantation.

Front: [Transplant] How does hyperacute transplant rejection differ from acute and chronic rejection?
Back:
Answer: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours due to preformed recipient antibodies. Acute rejection occurs days to months and often involves T cells and/or antibodies; chronic rejection develops over months to years with vascular narrowing and fibrosis.

Why it matters: Hyperacute rejection reflects preexisting antibodies and can begin during the transplant procedure. Acute and chronic processes develop later; T cells are important in acute cellular rejection, while chronic injury causes fibrosis and vascular narrowing.

Front: [Drugs] What is the target of rituximab?
Back:
Answer: CD20 on B cells; it is used for B-cell malignancies and autoimmune conditions.

Why it matters: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells; it does not target mature plasma cells, which generally lack CD20. It is used in B-cell malignancies and several autoimmune diseases.

Front: [Markers] What do CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19/CD20, and CD16/CD56 identify?
Back:
Answer: CD3: T cells; CD4: helper T cells; CD8: cytotoxic T cells; CD19/CD20: B cells; CD16/CD56: NK cells.

Why it matters: These surface markers identify broad lymphocyte lineages in flow cytometry. CD3/CD4/CD8 indicate T-cell populations; CD19/CD20 identify B cells; CD16/CD56 identify NK cells.

Front: [Drugs] Which agents target TNF-alpha and what conditions may they treat?
Back:
Answer: Infliximab and adalimumab are anti-TNF antibodies; etanercept is a soluble TNF-receptor fusion protein. These agents treat conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and IBD.

Why it matters: Infliximab and adalimumab neutralize TNF-alpha; etanercept acts as a soluble receptor decoy. Blocking TNF reduces inflammatory signaling in RA, IBD, and other immune-mediated disease.

PDF page(s): 31, 43

Front: [Drugs] What is the target of natalizumab, and what major risk is associated with it?
Back:
Answer: It blocks alpha-4 integrin and can be used for multiple sclerosis; it increases risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

Why it matters: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin-dependent leukocyte trafficking into the CNS. Reduced CNS immune surveillance raises risk of JC-virus reactivation and PML.

PDF page(s): 43

Front: [Tcells] Which immune cells are central to control of intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
Back:
Answer: Th1 CD4+ T cells activate infected macrophages via IFN-gamma; macrophages contain bacilli and can form granulomas.

Why it matters: TB bacilli can persist within macrophages, so macrophages need Th1-derived IFN-gamma activation to improve killing. The interaction can organize macrophages into granulomas that contain infection.
